# Two Years On: Follow-up of the Varden County Trial and a Subset of Halden Pilot Organisations

*Field report. A. Lindqvist, P. Mahony, D. Rao (Varden County Evaluation Unit / Easterly University) and R. Okafor (Halden Institute for Work Studies). Registered follow-up protocol VC-2023-04-F, filed at month 11.*

## Summary

We report 24-month outcomes from two sources: the Varden County cluster-randomised trial, whose case-processing offices remained on their assigned schedules for two years, and 14 organisations from the Halden pilot that hold record-based output data. In Varden case-processing offices, the gain in output per actual hour relative to control fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data, and output per employee stood at −3.4% (95% CI −8.0 to +1.2). The gain has therefore declined but not disappeared. A registered mediation test confirms that the reduction in recurring meetings accounts for 47% (95% CI 28 to 66%) of the per-hour gain; improved fatigue accounts for 18% (2 to 34%). The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12 because of waiting times. Three of the 14 Halden organisations have reverted, all with client-facing or coverage obligations.

## 1. Background

The nine-month report of the Varden trial left three questions to be settled at follow-up: whether the per-hour gain in case-processing would persist; whether the meetings association, found in an unregistered analysis, would survive a registered test; and whether timesheets understated the work actually done. Two subsequent publications bear on the first two. A re-analysis of the Halden pilot argued that per-hour gains in reduced-hours schemes are entirely an artifact of measurement, selection and novelty, and that the meetings hypothesis was a post hoc story. A meta-analysis of 23 studies concluded that effects show no sign of decay, on the basis of four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months. We address each directly.

## 2. Varden County: design at 24 months

The seven treated and seven control case-processing offices kept their assigned schedules for 24 months. To address concern about unrecorded work, we added a second hours measure: active log-in time on the county's case-management system, which records time staff are working on cases whether or not they claim it on a timesheet. The mediation analysis was registered at month 11, before 24-month outcomes were available. It specified two mediators, weekly hours in recurring meetings (from calendar data) and a validated fatigue scale, and a single outcome, output per log-measured hour.

The counter and contact-centre arm was ended by the county at month 12. In months 10 to 12, average waiting time in treated counter offices was 7.3 minutes against 4.0 in control offices, and the county judged that restoring service would require 12% more staff, raising the cost per contact handled by an estimated 9%. Those offices returned to 37.5 hours.

## 3. Varden County: results

**Table 1. Case-processing offices, treated relative to control (difference-in-differences)**

| Outcome | 9 months | 24 months |
|---|---|---|
| Output per FTE | −2.1% (−6.8 to +2.6) | −3.4% (−8.0 to +1.2) |
| Actual hours, timesheets | −13% | −12% |
| Actual hours, system logs | — | −11% |
| Output per hour, timesheets | +12.5% (+6.9 to +18.4) | +9.8% (+4.6 to +15.2) |
| Output per hour, system logs | — | +8.5% (+3.4 to +13.8) |
| Appeal overturn rate (treated v control) | 3.1% v 3.0% | 3.2% v 3.0% |
| Sick days per FTE | −29% | −27% |
| Annual resignations (treated v control) | 3.9% v 7.4% | 4.1% v 7.9% |

Log data show slightly more work than timesheets: actual hours fell by 11% on logs and 12% on timesheets, so the per-hour gain on the stricter measure is 8.5%. That gain is smaller than at nine months but its confidence interval excludes zero by a clear margin. Output per employee remains slightly below control; the hours reduction is mostly, not fully, offset.

The decline from 12.5% to 9.8% on the like-for-like timesheet measure is consistent with some fading of an initial effect. It is not consistent with the gain falling to zero by month ten, as an extrapolation of self-reported energy in the Halden data had suggested.

### Mediation

Recurring meeting time in treated case-processing offices fell from 7.4 to 3.9 hours per week per person between baseline and month 24; in control offices it moved from 7.2 to 7.0. Fatigue scores improved by 0.34 standard deviations in treated offices relative to control.

**Table 2. Registered mediation analysis, output per log-measured hour, 24 months**

| Pathway | Share of per-hour gain explained (95% CI) |
|---|---|
| Reduction in recurring meetings | 47% (28 to 66) |
| Improvement in fatigue | 18% (2 to 34) |
| Unexplained | 35% |

The meetings pathway, first suggested in the nine-month report's exploratory analysis and since dismissed as post hoc, survives a registered test with a larger sample of office-months and a pre-specified model. Reduced fatigue contributes, but less than half as much. About a third of the gain is not explained by either measured pathway.

### An unplanned observation

In month 15, two control offices, on their own initiative and without changing hours, carried out a "meeting audit" and cancelled a number of standing meetings. Recurring meeting time in those two offices fell from 7.1 to 5.0 hours per week, and their output per hour over the following six months was 4.1% above their own previous six months. This is two offices, uncontrolled, and the change was smaller than in treated offices. It suggests, without establishing, that part of the per-hour gain might be available without reducing hours. Whether reorganisation alone could capture most of the gain, or whether the hours cut is what makes such reorganisation happen and stick, cannot be determined from this trial, since no arm reorganised without reducing hours.

## 4. Halden organisations at 24 months

We contacted the 23 Halden organisations that had submitted output records; 14 agreed to provide 24-month data. Three of these had reverted to a five-day schedule: a hospitality group and a retail chain, both citing coverage of opening hours, and a marketing agency citing client deadlines. Their record-based output indices at the time of reversion were between 88 and 91.

Among the 11 that continued, record-based output at 24 months stood at 96.8 against the pre-pilot baseline, and actual hours from time tracking at 34.9 against 40.3 (−13.4%), an implied gain in output per actual hour of 11.8%. These organisations have no comparison group and are survivors twice over: they completed the pilot and then chose to continue. Their figures are an upper bound for organisations that self-select into reduced hours and find it suits them, not an estimate for organisations in general.

## 5. Bearing on earlier claims

**The re-analysis's claim that per-hour gains are entirely an artifact.** The Varden 24-month estimate uses record-based output, log-measured hours, randomised comparison and a two-year horizon, the standards that re-analysis itself recommended, and finds a gain of 8.5% (3.4 to 13.8). The re-analysis was right about the measurement problems it identified and right that headline figures were inflated; its conclusion that nothing remains once those problems are corrected is not supported.

**The meta-analysis's claim that effects show no sign of decay.** The four studies with follow-up beyond 12 months, listed in the meta-analysis's supplementary table, were all uncontrolled and all used scheduled hours. Their pooled estimate therefore reflects the design features the meta-analysis itself found to inflate effects, and it cannot speak to decay. In the one controlled study with long follow-up, this one, the per-hour gain declined by about a quarter between nine and 24 months.

## 6. Limitations

One public employer; seven offices per arm in the case-processing stratum. Mediation analysis assumes no unmeasured confounding between mediators and outcome, which a cluster trial cannot guarantee. The Halden subset is small and self-selected. Neither source extends beyond 24 months.

response:
This is a strong follow-up. It does what the nine-month report promised:
- It added a second hours measure (system logs) to capture unrecorded work.
- It reported baseline meeting time, which the nine-month analysis lacked.
- It registered the mediation test before the 24-month outcomes were available.
- It reports a decline in the effect rather than hiding it.
- It labels the Halden subset as "survivors twice over."

Its responses to the re-analysis and the meta-analysis are mostly fair. The main problems are a misleading comparison in the Summary, a confound in the decay estimate that the paper doesn't notice, and some overstatement of the mediation result.

## Arithmetic check

Most figures are consistent:
- Varden at 24 months: output per hour on timesheets is 0.966/0.88 = +9.8%, and on logs 0.966/0.89 = +8.5%.
- Halden continuers: hours ratio 34.9/40.3 = 0.866 (−13.4%), and 0.968/0.866 = +11.8%.
- Mediation shares add to 100%.

The decline: on a like-for-like basis, 12.5% → 9.8% is a fall of about 22%. That is "about a quarter" only loosely.

## 1. The Summary compares two different measures

The Summary says the gain "fell from 12.5% at nine months to 8.5% at 24 months, measured with system log data." The 12.5% is a timesheet figure; the 8.5% is a log figure. Comparing them mixes the change in measure with the change over time. The like-for-like figures are **12.5% → 9.8%** on timesheets. The body of the paper gets this right, so the Summary should match it.

The two estimates' confidence intervals also overlap almost completely (+6.9 to +18.4 at nine months, +4.6 to +15.2 at 24 months), and the decline is never tested. "Consistent with some fading" is fair. The data can't show how much fading occurred, or whether any did.

## 2. Control-arm contamination affects the decay estimate

The "unplanned observation" is reported as suggestive evidence about meetings. It also bears on the decay estimate, and the paper doesn't connect the two.

From month 15, two of the seven control offices cut their meetings and raised output per hour by 4.1%. That raises the control mean by roughly 2/7 × 4.1 ≈ 1.2 points over months 15–24. In a difference-in-differences design, a better control arm looks like a smaller treatment effect. That 1.2 points could account for a substantial part of the 2.7-point "decline."

I'd add two sensitivity checks:
- The 24-month estimate with those two offices excluded, or with their post-audit months excluded.
- The treated offices' trajectory against their own pre-period.

If the decline mostly disappears, the paper's evidence on decay changes. The finding would become "little fading in the treated offices." It would no longer be "about a quarter."

## 3. The mediation result is stronger than an exploratory finding, but "confirms" goes too far

- **Same offices that generated the hypothesis.** The test was registered at month 11, after the nine-month exploratory correlation, and uses the same seven treated offices. The later months add data, but the units are the same. It is a pre-specified test of the hypothesis, not an independent replication.
- **Effective sample size.** "A larger sample of office-months" adds observations, but the units that were randomised are still 14 offices. Fairly tight intervals (28–66%) from 14 clusters need justification. How were standard errors clustered, and was a small-cluster correction applied?
- **Timing.** The paper doesn't say whether the mediators were measured before the outcome or at the same time. Mediation estimates are much weaker when they are measured together.
- **Comparing the two pathways.** "Less than half as much" compares point estimates (18% vs 47%). The intervals overlap (2–34 vs 28–66), and the difference isn't tested.
- **Assumptions.** The Limitations section notes the no-unmeasured-confounding assumption. A plausible confounder is office-manager quality: a good manager might both cut meetings and raise output. That deserves naming, and the Summary's "confirms" should be softened to "supports."

## 4. What the log measure captures

The meeting pathway is estimated on "output per log-measured hour," where logs record "active log-in time on the case-management system." If logs capture only time spent on cases, meetings never enter the denominator. Cutting meetings would then not raise output per log-hour mechanically, and the 47% would need a different explanation.

The numbers also don't fit a case-work-only reading. In treated offices, meetings fell about 3.5 hours a week while total timesheet hours fell about 12% (roughly 4.5 hours). Non-meeting time therefore fell only about 3%. Yet log hours fell 11%.

The paper should define exactly what log time includes. That definition determines how both the hours result and the mediation result should be read.

## 5. Two issues from the nine-month report remain open

- **Cost.** Timesheet hours fell 12% against a scheduled cut of 20%, so about 3 hours a week of claimed overtime appears to persist after two years, on top of unchanged pay. Output per FTE is −3.4%. Cost per case has almost certainly risen. For a county deciding whether to keep the schedule, that is the decision-relevant figure, and it still isn't reported.
- **Backlogs and deadlines.** The nine-month Limitations raised whether backlogs would build past statutory deadlines. The case-management system holds that data, but it isn't reported. Overturn rates (3.2% vs 3.0%) also still lack confidence intervals.

## 6. The counter-arm cost figure needs a derivation

The county estimated that restoring service needs 12% more staff, raising cost per contact by about 9%. If those staff are paid the same and contacts handled return to roughly control levels, cost per contact should rise by about 12%. That is what you get from 1.12 × 0.83 hours × 1.067 per-hour productivity ≈ 0.99 of control output, at 1.12 times the cost. The 9% may reflect cheaper part-time staff or rising demand, but it should be shown.

## 7. The Halden section

- **A reversion that doesn't fit the framing.** The Summary says all three reverting organisations had "client-facing or coverage obligations." One was a **marketing agency** citing client deadlines. That is discretionary work in the meta-analysis's terms, and marketing was one of Halden's knowledge-work sectors. Grouping it with retail and hospitality makes the work-type pattern look cleaner than it is. It should be reported as a reversion in discretionary work.
- **Timing.** Halden originally reported five reversions at the end of the pilot (retail, hospitality and healthcare administration). The paper should say whether these three are among those five or are new reversions.
- **Non-response.** Nine of the 23 organisations contacted declined to provide data. If struggling organisations were less willing to share, the 11 continuers are selected a third time.
- **"Upper bound."** This isn't guaranteed. With no comparison group over more than two years, general changes in the economy could push output per hour either way. New software tools are one example. "Upper bound" depends on selection being the only bias.
- **Baseline.** The 40.3-hour baseline is the 27-organisation figure from Varga & Holm. The 11-organisation subset should use its own baseline.

## 8. Smaller points

- **Sick days (−27%).** The point I raised for the meta-analysis applies here. If the 30-hour week means fewer working days, sick days per FTE fall mechanically. The figure should be expressed per scheduled day.
- **Source of the baseline meeting figures.** The nine-month report said calendar data were collected only in month six. The 7.4- and 7.2-hour baselines presumably come from retrospective calendar extraction. The paper should say so.
- **Independence.** This report is written by the authors of both original studies, and it responds to their critics. It does so fairly. Even so, an independent re-analysis of the 24-month data, of the kind the Halden data-sharing policy made possible, would strengthen it.

## The responses to earlier claims

- **The re-analysis ("entirely an artifact").** The rebuttal is sound. One randomised estimate that meets the re-analysis's own standards (record-based output, measured hours, randomised comparison, long follow-up) and excludes zero is enough to refute "entirely." It doesn't establish how far the result generalises beyond one public employer.
- **The meta-analysis ("no sign of decay").** The rebuttal confirms the concern I raised earlier: all four long-follow-up studies were uncontrolled and used scheduled hours. The paper's own counter-evidence, a decline of about a quarter, should carry the caveat from point 2, since some of that decline may come from the control arm improving.

## Where the evidence stands now

- **Per-hour gains in discretionary work are real and persist to two years**, at about 8–10% in the best-measured case. Some fading is possible, but how much is uncertain and partly confounded by the control offices' changes.
- **Per-employee output in discretionary work** is slightly below control (about −2% to −3%), and the gap is not statistically significant. Cost per unit of output has probably risen, but this hasn't been measured.
- **Coverage-bound work** has a clear answer. Service worsens unless staff are added, and the one randomised arm was stopped.
- **Mechanism.** Cutting meetings is now the leading candidate, with pre-registered support. Fatigue plays a smaller role. About a third of the gain is unexplained. The key open question is the one the paper itself names: could reorganisation without cutting hours capture most of the gain? Only a trial with a reorganise-only arm can answer it.

I can draft referee comments, a corrected Summary, or a design sketch for a three-arm trial (reduced hours, meeting reform only, control) that would answer that question.
